A B S T R A C T
Nanobubble water (NBW) contains 106–108 gas bubbles per milliliter with diameter < 1 µm. These ﬁne bubbles
possess high mass transfer eﬃciency and hydrophobic property beneﬁcial for agricultural and biomedical ap-
plication. Nowadays, much attention has been paid to the secure and sustainable management of lignocellulosic
wastes. Cellulose is regarded as one kind of slowly biodegradable organic components owing to its complex
crystalline structure. This study investigated the eﬀect of O2-containing gas NBW on anaerobic digestion (AD) of
cellulose for methane production. Results show that the cumulative methane yields from the reactors with Air-
NBW (193 NmL/g-VSreduced), N2-NBW (196 NmL/g-VSreduced) and O2-NBW (233 NmL/g-VSreduced) addition were
increased by 8–30% in comparison to the control (with the same amount of deionized water addition) (179
NmL/g-VSreduced). Under NBW addition, the reductions in cellulose content and cellulose crystallinity were re-
spectively enhanced by 8–14% and 9–21% during AD, in which cellulase activity was elevated by 10–38%. The
O2-NBW reactor was found to have the highest electron transport system activity, increasing by 1.7 times
compared to the control, most probably due to the collapse of O2-nanobubbles and release of O2 resulting in
micro-oxygen environment under the test condition. Besides, microbial community analysis suggests that the
direct interspecies electron transfer could be quickly established with the addition of NBW. Results from this
study also shed light on the mechanisms involved in the bioconversion of cellulose to methane via AD sup-
plemented with NBW.

1. Introduction
Fossil fuel is still the main source of global energy, contributing to
both greenhouse gases emission and worse regional air quality. A robust
global economic growth and increasing demand on temperature control
during daily life have driven the rapid growth of global energy con-
sumption. European Biogas Association (EBA) has developed a coherent
strategy for realizing the optimal use of biogas, syngas and biomethane
from anaerobic digestion (AD) and biomass gasiﬁcation to face energy
crisis and environmental pollution [1]. In this context, there is a great
demand for seeking the clean or pollution free methods to enhance
methane production from AD of various organic solid wastes.
Lignocellulose is one kind of polymeric materials with intricate
three-dimensional network, in which the content of cellulose is up to
50% [2]. The secure and sustainable management of lignocellulosic
biomass has also been considered as a prominent alternative for pet-
roleum [3]. In addition, biomethane production from lignocellulosic
biomass through AD process has become more attractive due to its
environmental sustainability and low cost [4]. To improve AD eﬃ-
ciency of lignocellulose, various pretreatments have been attempted,
including physical, chemical and biological methods. For instance,
hydrothermal pretreatment of lignocellulosic biomass gained the
highest biodegradability and biochemical methane potential [5]. Sam-
busiti et al. claimed that alkaline pretreatment could enhance the me-
thane production from lignocellulose [6]. Methane production from
lignocellulose can also be enhanced after pretreatment by a pure strain
Bacillus Subtilis [7]. Although the above-mentioned methods can
achieve some improvement on methane production from AD of lig-
nocellulosic materials, the increment of methane yield is diﬃcult to
balance the possible secondary pollution and the high operation cost,
mainly due to the large amount of chemicals addition and/or additional
energy consumption in these pretreatments.
Most recently, the advancements in micro-oxygen technology reﬂect
great potentials to address the low hydrolysis rate of highly recalcitrant
feedstocks (like lignocellulosic biomass in this study) [8] and low me-
tabolic activity of microbes [9]. In general, oxidation-reduction po-
tential (ORP) value in the range of 0 to −470 mV can be deﬁned as
micro-oxygen environment that could improve methane yield and vo-
latile fatty acids (VFAs) production to a certain extent in AD process
[8,10]. Hydrolysis is the rate-limiting AD step of refractory substrates
such as lignocellulosic biomass [11]. The underlying rationale of an
enhanced AD process is usually relating to the augmentation of mi-
crobial diversity and activity (facultative heterotrophs) resulting in
improved hydrolysis of substrate [10]. For example, the micro-aerobic
AD system was detected to have a higher proportion of Firmicutes
phylum associated with a higher substrate hydrolysis rate [8]. An in-
termittent micro-aeration system can also accelerate VFAs conversion
by facultative bacteria and improve methane yield by hydrogenotrophic
methanogens, respectively [10]. In order to achieve the micro-aeration
purpose, high costs are required for electricity and maintenance of the
mechanical parts when conventional mechanical aerator or diﬀuser
systems are applied [12]. On the other hand, some chemical oxidants
(i.e. H2O2 and calcium peroxide) can release peroxides to react with
water and elevate O2 levels, but they also kill the microbes and pollute
aquatic ecosystems [13]. All these works indicate that the micro-aera-
tion biotechnology would be more promising if it is non-toxic with no
chemical addition, especially for the enhancement of AD process, in
order to meet the sustainable development goals (SDGs).
Nanobubble water (NBW) contains 106–108 ﬁne bubbles per milli-
liter with diameter < 1 μm [14], which can induce many intriguing
properties. These nanobubbles (NBs) possess high mass transfer eﬃ-
ciency, high surface area, and long residence time [15]. NBs in NBW
can increase the contact surface area between the liquid and solid
phases. The hydrophobic attraction force property of NBs is also helpful
for them to adhere onto the solid surface, thus promoting mass transfer,
chemical reactions and metabolism [16]. NBW can be relatively stably
stored for three months [17], thus it is likely able to maintain a long-
lasting O2 concentration if being added into AD reactors. Air-NBW was
presumed to create micro-oxygen environment that greatly improved
the hydrolysis-acidiﬁcation stage of high cellulose loading AD [18]. O2-
NBW was trialed to control methane emission from algae bloom waters
[19], which has also been found to augment the anaerobically digested
sludge and then improve methane production from corn straw [9]. In
addition, the mass transfer rate of O2 to the liquid phase in O2-NBW was
claimed to be 125 times faster than that of bulk bubble (diameter >
1000 nm) [20]. Seen from the above works, O2-containing gas NBW
has great potentials for enhanced AD of lignocellulosic biomass. How-
ever, whether O2-containing gas NBW can create a micro-oxygen en-
vironment or not remains unclear, and the underlying mechanisms for
the enhanced methane production from AD of lignocellulosic biomass
hasn’t been addressed so far. Most importantly, up to now, no reports
disclosed the exact role of O2 released by O2-NBW on microorganisms
and their metabolism in the micro-oxygen environment, in addition to
the eﬀect of O2 concentration in NBW on methane yield.
Therefore, the present work was designed to investigate the eﬀects
of diﬀerent O2-containing gas NBWs (Air-NBW, N2-NBW, O2-NBW, and
artiﬁcial N2/O2 gas mixture with diﬀerent mixing ratios) addition on
AD of cellulose. The main objectives of this study were: 1) to investigate
the eﬀects of NBW on electron transport system (ETS) and enzyme
activity during AD of cellulose under the addition of diﬀerent NBWs; 2)
to quantify the cellulose content and crystallinity reduction eﬃciency;
3) to verify O2-NBW’s function on biochemical methane potential
(BMP) using diﬀerent N2 and O2 gas mixture derived NBWs; and 4) to
elucidate the possible mechanisms by analyzing bacterial and archaeal
communities for a better understanding of methane production from
cellulose under NBW addition.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Materials

digested sludge was anaerobically digested at 35 ± 1 °C for one week
before BMP test. Cellulose used in this study was purchased from
Sigma-Aldrich (Avicel® PH-101), with an average particle diameter of
50 μm. The physicochemical properties of the cellulose and digested
sludge are shown in Table 1. The cellulose crystallinity is very high,

2.2. Preparation of NBW
NBW was prepared as previously described [18]. Brieﬂy, 1 L deio-
nized water (DW) in a 5 L plastic beaker was injected into the HACK
FB11-UFB generator (HACK UFB Co., Ltd., Yamanashi, Japan) with
diﬀerent gases to obtain ‘water containing NBs’, namely NBW. Gas in-
take speed and DW circulation ﬂow rate of the HACK FB11-UFB gen-
erator were controlled at 0.05 L/min and 3 L/min, respectively. The
NBW generation process lasted for 20 min at room temperature
(25 ± 1 °C). NBW was produced in a combination of pressurized
mechanical cyclic and spiral liquid ﬂow. One liter of air, N2, O2 or the
N2/O2 gas mixture at a diﬀerent volume ratio of 4:1, 1:1 or 1:3 was used
for NBW generation, respectively. The N2/O2 gas mixture was produced
by using a wet gas meter (W-NK-0.5, Shinagawa Co., Japan).
2.3. BMP tests
The BMP test was used to assess the biodegradability of cellulose
with NBW and DW addition. The tests were performed using 120 mL
closed Schott Duran serum bottles. Each bottle, with a working volume
of 70 mL, was ﬁrstly added with 35 mL of NBW or DW, then 35 mL of
inoculum with biodegradable substances removed, and at last, cellulose
at a concentration of 5 g/L, achieving a feed-to-microorganisms (F/M)
ratio of 1 g-volatile solids (VS)cellulose/g-VSinoculum with no addition of
other substances like macro- and/or micro-nutrients. As reported,
slightly alkaline condition can enhance the hydrolysis of cellulose [22],
the limiting step of AD. In our previous studies [14,18], under the ad-
dition of NBW, VFAs accumulation usually occur during the initial stage
of AD of waste activated sludge and cellulose, which may lead to an
acidic environment inﬂuencing the BMP tests. Thus, in this study, after
inoculation, the initial pH of the mixture was adjusted to 8.0 using
2.0 M NaOH or HCl to avoid (or alleviate) the above-mentioned VFAs
inhibition eﬀects on AD process. Then, the AD reactors were subjected
to 5 min of N2 ﬂushing to create anaerobic conditions. All the AD ex-
periments were conducted for 18 days in a temperature-controlled in-
cubator at 35 ± 1 °C, and all the tests were carried out in triplicate. Six
types of NBW derived from diﬀerent gases (air, N2, O2, and the N2/O2
gas mixture at ratios of 4:1, 1:1 and 1:3) were tested to investigate BMP
from cellulose. The reactors were labelled as Air-NBW, N2-NBW, O2-
NBW, N2/O2 (4:1)-NBW, N2/O2 (1:1)-NBW, N2/O2 (1:3)-NBW, respec-
tively. The addition of DW instead of NBW was used as control (DW
reactors). The reactors without cellulose addition (only inoculum and
NBW or DW) were conducted as blank to eliminate the methane amount
produced by the residual biodegradable organics in the inoculum under
NBW or DW addition. The methane yield from each blank was also
deducted from each treatment. The cumulative methane production
was calculated based on the reduced VS of cellulose. Net methane yield
(NmL/g-VSreduced) from cellulose at all conditions was calculated as
previously described [18]. The BMP in this study was expressed as the
volume of methane under standard conditions (1013 hPa, 273 K) as
described elsewhere [9].

3. Results and discussion
3.1. Micro-oxygen environment created by O2-NBW
Micro-oxygen environment has been claimed to have enhancement
eﬀect on methane yield from AD of lignocellulosic biomass [30]. In this
regard, the oxygen contained in NBs is diﬃcult to be detected by the
standard DO meter or Winkler oxygen titration method [15], although
the DO value of O2-NBW was slightly higher than Air-NBW and N2-NBW
after reaching stable (Fig. 1a). Since ORP has a linear relationship with
the logarithm of oxygen concentration, and a DO of 0.1 mg/L is
equivalent to an ORP of −96 mV in the aqueous phase [10], ORP value
in the range of 0 to −470 mV is deﬁned as micro-oxygen environment
[8,10]. In this study, the highest ORP value was detected in the O2-NBW

reported, the optimal ORP for methanogens is lower than −350 mV
[31], indicating that the micro-oxygen environment brought about by
O2-NBW addition may not inhibit the AD of cellulose to produce me-
thane. The observations on DO and ORP changes in this study are si-
milar with the O2-NBW applications in the remediation of anaerobic
environment by Wang et al. [32], in which O2-NBW was found to
prolong the survival time of aerobic zebraﬁsh due to the O2 released
from O2-NB. Results from this study indicate that O2-NBW may provide
a micro-oxygen environment that would enhance methane production
from AD of lignocellulosic biomass.

3.4. INT-electron transport system activities in BMP tests
The microbial bioactivity during the 18 days’ AD with NBW addi-
tion were assessed by monitoring the electron transport rate during the
microbial metabolism. It is correlated with intracellular ETS through
measuring the rate of INT reducing 2-(p-iodophenyl)-3-(p-nitrophenyl)-
5-phenyl tetrazolium chloride formazan (INTF) by providing a super
electron donor (NADH and succinic acid) [29]. In this study, as shown
in Fig. 3b, initially the ETS activity increased rapidly in all the reactors,
which was consistent with the cellulase activity changes in these AD
systems. The highest ETS activity was detected in the O2-NBW reactor
on day 4, reaching 247.2 mg/(g·h), which was approximately 1.7 times
that of the DW reactor, followed by N2-NBW (1.6 times) and Air-NBW
(1.1 times) reactors (Fig. 3b). It has been conﬁrmed that the ETS ac-
tivity is closely associated with the methanogenic eﬃciency (Fig. 5a).
ETS generally occurs in the cell membrane of bacteria [35]. It can
transfer electrons from the coenzymes produced by the Szent-Györgyi-
Krebs cycle (NADH, NADPH) to the terminal electron acceptor in the
oxidative phosphorylation (electron transport) pathway. The surface of
NBs has negative charges [16], which could attract NAD+; NBs also
have higher speed of motion, favoring the movement of NAD+ that is
used for reduction reaction to generate NADH. This might be the reason
why NBW addition promoted the ETS in the reactors (Fig. 6). Ahmed
et al. found that NBW could contribute to seed germination and plant
growth [36], possibly due to the promotion eﬀect of NBs on ETS ac-
tivity.
O2 can increase ETS activity because O2 may easily act as an elec-
tron acceptor in ETS [35]. A signiﬁcant amount of energy can be re-
leased by the reduction of O2 with NADH, which then produces a
proton gradient that drives the synthesis of ATP and the transport of
other metabolites (Fig. 6). These deductions associated with ETS
changes also suggest that the O2-NBW reactor may have higher po-
tential for creating micro-oxygen environment than other reactors,
which might be one major reason for the more enhanced methane
production from the O2-NBW reactor. Still, future research is de-
manding on more direct evidence for synthesis of ATP and the transport
of other metabolites under NBW addition condition. The positive eﬀect
of NBW addition on ETS activity indicates that NBW could increase the
bioactivity of microbes by accelerating the electron transport, and then
contribute to the enriched microbial community.

3.6. Methane production
3.6.1. Methane yield from AD of cellulose under NBW addition
The daily methane productions from the DW, Air-NBW, N2-NBW,
O2-NBW, N2/O2 (4:1)-NBW, N2/O2 (1:1)-NBW and N2/O2 (1:3)-NBW

N2/O2 (1:3)-NBW reactors; then their daily methane productions de-
creased. After day 16, the daily methane productions gradually de-
creased to 0 in all the reactors.
Fig. 5a shows that the cumulative methane yields from cellulose in
the DW, Air-NBW, N2-NBW and O2-NBW reactors varied during the
18 days’ batch BMP tests. In the ﬁrst two days, little methane produc-
tion was detected from the NBW addition reactors, which is similar with
that of the DW reactor. After that, their methane productions increased
remarkably until day 14 when their cumulative methane yields became
level oﬀ. During the 18 days’ BMP, the cumulative methane yields from
cellulose in the O2-NBW, N2-NBW and Air-NBW reactors reached
233.0 ± 6.2, 196.1 ± 1.4, and 193.3 ± 4.5 NmL/g-VSreduced, in-
creasing by 29.9%, 9.3% and 7.7% compared with that from the DW
reactor (179.4 ± 2.4 NmL/g-VSreduced). In this study, the highest cu-
mulative methane yield was achieved from the O2-NBW reactor, most
probably attributable to the enriched microbial community (as noted in
3.5), thus enhanced decomposition of cellulose. To clarify the eﬀect of
O2 content in NBW on BMP, the N2 and O2 gas mixture NBW was ex-
amined through the BMP of cellulose at diﬀerent mixing ratios
(Fig. 5b). As expected, the highest methane yield was achieved from the
N2/O2 (1:3)-NBW reactor, followed by N2/O2 (1:1)-NBW and N2/O2
(4:1)-NBW reactors. Results show that the NBW with the highest O2
content (O2-NBW) performed best in the methane production from AD
of cellulose (Fig. 5b).
3.6.2. Analysis based on the modiﬁed Gompertz model
The simulated maximum cumulative methane yields (M0) are very
similar to the experimental methane yields, indicating that the AD of
cellulose can be perfectly ﬁtted by the modiﬁed Gompertz equation
(Fig. S6), with a high correlation coeﬃcient (R2) ranging from 0.995 to
0.999. Table 2 also lists the model-based best-ﬁt evaluation of kinetic
parameters. The maximum methane production rate (μm) increased in
the reactors with NBW addition compared with that in the DW reactor,
indicating their enhanced AD eﬃciency. However, AD with NBW ad-
dition showed a little bit longer lag phase time (λ) than the DW reactor,
possibly due to that the anaerobic microorganisms need a short adap-
tion period to accommodate the new environment created in the re-
actors by NBW addition. In this table, the theoretical methane yield
(TMY) was calculated based on the chemical formula of cellulose
((C6H10O5)n); and BD represents the biodegradability of cellulose
during the AD process, which was calculated by the ratio of EMY to
TMY. The BD value can be also used to predict the overall enhancement
on energy recovery and to better assess the degradation of organic
matter during AD process. A maximum BD value of 56.2% was achieved
in the O2-NBW reactor, followed by N2/O2 (1:3)-NBW (51.2%), N2/O2
(1:1)-NBW (49.1%), N2/O2 (4:1)-NBW (48.6%), N2-NBW (47.3%), Air-
NBW (46.6%) and DW (43.2%) reactors (Table 2), respectively. The
results reﬂect that methane production from cellulose was enhanced
with the addition of NBW.
3.7. Preliminary analysis on mechanisms
The pathways involved in the application of NBW for enhanced
methane production from cellulose are illustrated in Fig. 6. The oligo-
saccharide layer produced during the ﬁrst-stage of AD, namely, hy-
drolysis of cellulose particles exhibits a low diﬀusion eﬃciency. The
cellulose particles are surrounded in a layer form, resulting in mass
transfer resistance and hindered decomposition of cellulose particles
[21]. In this study, the hydrophilic and negatively charged surfaces of
O2-NBs, Air-NBs or N2-NBs can attract H+ and NAD+, then help to
attack the oligosaccharide layer by cellulolytic and microorganisms
together with cellulase due to the largely increased surface and contact
area. The destruction of the oligosaccharide layer may enhance the
hydrolysis of cellulose through cellulase activity. The O2-NBW reactor
gained the highest ETS activity owing to the collapse of O2-NBs and
release of O2, which can provide a micro-oxygen environment that
drives the synthesis of ATP and increases the biological activity. Results
from the microbial community structure analysis suggest that the
micro-oxygen environment might promote the hydrolysis stage of AD.
Besides, NBW addition can also enhance metabolisms of microbes in-
cluding hydrogenotrophic and acetoclastic methanogens, further im-
proving methane production from cellulose.
4. Conclusions
The present study provided a promising approach to increase me-
thane yield from AD of cellulose through micro-oxygen environment
provided by O2-NBW. In agreement with the hypothesis, O2-containing
gas NBW supplementation improved methane production from cellu-
lose during AD. 8%–30% increase of methane yield and 8%–14% in-
crease of cellulose reduction were achieved from AD of cellulose with
NBW addition compared to the control (DW addition). Cellulase ac-
tivity, cellulose crystallinity reduction and ETS activity were also en-
hanced under NBW addition. O2-containing gas NBW addition was
found to enrich facultative bacteria and hydrogenotrophic methano-
gens. In this study, we ﬁrst conﬁrmed that O2-NBW could provide
micro-oxygen environment which has positive eﬀects on methane
production from cellulose in the lab-scale tests. Results from this work
can also help us better comprehend the fundamentals involved. As seen,
O2-containing gas NBW can create micro-oxygen environment that is
conductive to enhanced methane production with no chemical addition
and possibly no additional energy consumption during AD. Future
